claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.

Integrating high-resolution microstructural characterization with machine-learning surrogate models enables accurate prediction of the tensile and fracture properties of hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
The integrated method predicts mechanical properties more rapidly than traditional first-principles and CALPHAD-based methods.
Descriptors extracted from TEM, atom-probe tomography, and nanoindentation data can be used to train surrogates for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
The spatial distribution of the hierarchical heterostructure and phase coexistence govern local mechanical responses.
High-resolution imaging captures spatial and chemical heterogeneities relevant to local mechanical response.
A machine-learning model can identify statistically significant microstructural descriptors that correlate with local mechanical responses.
Using descriptor-based surrogates avoids full-scale high-fidelity simulations and decreases computational load without sacrificing prediction fidelity.
The method will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness within ±10% of experimental measurements.
The method will reduce computational runtime by more than 50-fold relative to traditional first-principles and CALPHAD approaches.
Traditional first-principles calculations and CALPHAD analyses are computationally prohibitive for this prediction task.
Traditional and unaugmented machine-learning methods have limited success in predicting toughness.
Insufficient microstructural resolution will reduce reliability because key heterogeneities will not be captured.
Aging, phase separation, or unexpected secondary phases can make the model unreliable by causing the hierarchical structure to deviate from its training domain.
The expected accuracy and efficiency gains depend on the quality and representativeness of the microstructural inputs.
